title: Self-assembly Monte Carlo reveals localized entanglement in giant polymer melts
authors: Enrico Fornasa, Francesco Slongo, Cristian Micheletti
abstract: Topological entanglements are central to understanding and predicting the properties of polymer melts. Yet, they make equilibrium sampling computationally challenging, as decorrelation times grow rapidly with chain length. Here, we introduce a Monte Carlo scheme that bypasses typical computational bottlenecks by working in a self-assembly ensemble rather than at fixed composition. Strictly local moves efficiently propagate backbone reconnections across scales while conserving the number of linear chains, achieving near-linear scaling of decorrelation time with system size, $τ_{\rm eq}\sim V^{1.0}$. With this method, formulated for a fully-packed lattice, we equilibrate periodic systems totalling up to $\simeq 1.1\times 10^9$ monomers, accessing a universal melt regime insensitive to lattice details. We analyze intra- and inter-chain entanglements for chains of up to $N\simeq 5 \times 10^5$ monomers, revealing that they manifest as localized knots and links rather than as global tangles. Finally, we show that the magnitude of the Gauss linking integral between neighbouring chains grows only as $N^{1/4}$.
summary: This work introduces a novel Self-Assembly Monte Carlo method to simulate polymer melts, overcoming severe computational barriers associated with topological entanglement. The method efficiently samples large systems, revealing that polymer entanglements are localized knots rather than global tangles. This advances the understanding of polymer physics by providing a scalable simulation tool for complex topological matter.
main_problem: Understanding the topological entanglements governing the properties of polymer melts, which are computationally challenging to sample due to rapidly growing decorrelation times.
main_result: The authors developed a Self-Assembly Monte Carlo scheme that achieves near-linear scaling of decorrelation time ($	au_{eq} \sim V^{1.0}$), revealing that entanglements manifest as localized knots and links rather than global tangles.
method: A specialized Monte Carlo simulation ensemble (Self-Assembly Monte Carlo) that works by fluctuating composition while conserving local connectivity, bypassing bottlenecks of fixed-composition methods.
model_or_system: The study models polymer melts using a fully-packed lattice system composed of giant linear chains and a ring background.
key_observables: Decorrelation time ($	au_{eq}$), intra- and inter-chain entanglements (knots/links), Gauss linking integral, and the volume fraction of linear chains ($\phi_{lin}$).
important_parameters: System size ($V$), chain length ($N$), and the characteristic length scale for knot formation ($ ar{N}_{	ext{tref}} \simeq 4998$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the system reaches a universal melt regime insensitive to lattice details, although a general proof of ergodicity for the SAMC scheme is noted as lacking.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the linear scaling of $	au_{eq}$ with volume, the emergence of giant linear components occupying $\sim 90\%$ of the volume, and probability distributions for knot types and linking integrals.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the SAMC method to overcome sampling bottlenecks in polymer melts. It then analyzes the scaling of decorrelation time and the macroscopic structure, concluding with detailed topological analyses of localized knots and the scaling of linking integrals.
why_interesting: The development of an efficient simulation technique for complex topological systems, like polymer melts, provides advanced numerical tools applicable to other non-equilibrium or highly constrained many-body systems.

For clarity, the sketch is shown for a blend with n = 2 linear chains on a two-dimensional (8 × 8) periodic square lattice. First, an endpoint A is randomly chosen among the 2n = 4 degree-1 sites (open circles). Next, a site B is randomly chosen among the non-bonded nearest neighbours of A. Then, a site C is randomly chosen among the bonded neighbours of B. If C is an endpoint, the move is rejected, otherwise bond BC is replaced by AB, obtaining the evolved configuration shown on the right. (a) Wrapped and (b) unwrapped representations of an SAMC-equilibrated configuration with n = 10 linear chains on a fully-packed 1024 × 1024 × 1024 periodic lattice, totalling ≃1.1 × 109 monomers.
